rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Confusion: Students often think insulators and semiconductors are fundamentally different materials — they are the SAME band structure, just with different $E_g$ values. Diamond ($5.5\,\text{eV}$) is an insulator, silicon ($1.12\,\text{eV}$) is a semiconductor; both have the diamond crystal structure.  ·  Confusion: Metals do NOT have a band gap. The Fermi level lies inside a band. There is no "forbidden gap" separating valence from conduction band — they are the same band or overlapping bands.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Confusion: In metals, conductivity decreases with temperature because more phonons scatter electrons. In semiconductors, conductivity increases because more carriers are generated. Students mix up the direction of temperature dependence.  ·  Confusion: The Fermi level in an intrinsic semiconductor lies near the MIDDLE of the band gap, not at the bottom of the conduction band. $E_F \approx E_g/2 + (k_B T/2) \ln(N_v/N_c)$. This is crucial for understanding doping effects.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Fact (Historical): The band theory explanation of metals, insulators, and semiconductors was developed by Felix Bloch (1928), Alan Wilson (1931), and Rudolf Peierls. It unified the electrical properties of solids under a single quantum-mechanical framework.  ·  Fact (Application): The temperature dependence of semiconductor resistance is used in thermistors (temperature sensors). NTC (negative temperature coefficient) thermistors use semiconductors; PTC (positive) thermistors use metals or special ceramics.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Metals – band overlap or partial filling:** In metals, the valence band is either partially filled (alkali metals like Na, K have one electron per atom in an s-band) OR it overlaps with the conduction band (alkaline earth metals like Mg). In both cases, the Fermi level $E_F$ lies within a band, so electrons have empty states immediately available at $E_F$.…  ·  **Insulators – wide band gap:** In insulators (diamond, SiO$_2$, NaCl), the valence band is completely filled and the conduction band is completely empty at 0 K. The band gap $E_g > 3\,\text{eV}$ (typically 5–10 eV). At room temperature, $k_B T \approx 0.026\,\text{eV} \ll E_g$, so thermal excitation across the gap is negligible. No carriers $\rightarrow$ no conduction.  ·  **Semiconductors – small band gap:** In semiconductors (Si, Ge, GaAs), the band gap is small ($E_g \approx 0.5\text{--}3\,\text{eV}$). At room temperature, a small but significant number of electrons are thermally excited from the valence band to the conduction band, leaving holes in the valence band.…

rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Difference between metals, insulators and semiconductors using band theory and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Difference between metals, insulators and semiconductors using band theory  ·  Confusion: Holes are NOT real particles. They are quasiparticles representing collective motion of electrons in a nearly-full band. They have positive charge, but they are not positrons (antimatter).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Confusion: A partially filled valence band and a completely filled valence band with overlap to a conduction band are both metallic. The distinction is subtle — in the first case, there is one band partially filled; in the second, two bands overlap, so electrons can move freely into the higher band.  ·  Confusion: Germanium has higher intrinsic carrier concentration than silicon at room temperature because its band gap is smaller ($0.67\,\text{eV}$ vs $1.12\,\text{eV}$), so thermal excitation is more probable. But Si is more widely used because it forms a stable native oxide (SiO$_2$).  ·  Confusion: The band gap of a semiconductor is temperature dependent. $E_g$ decreases as temperature increases (lattice expansion, electron-phonon coupling). This means the temperature coefficient of resistance has contributions from both carrier generation and gap narrowing.
